fields.description:
## Problem

The repo already has a strong agent foundation: root/package `AGENTS.md`, scoped PR rules, PR review, PR fix, docs review, auto re-review, and fail-closed structured-output checks. But the system is **reactive** — it acts at PR time, after the code already exists. Rule quality is hand-curated, recurring review findings aren't systematically mined, and lessons from reviews, fixes, and refactors aren't fed back into durable guardrails. The same judgment is also applied at only one point in the lifecycle (review), never while code is being written.

The deeper issue this creates: **senior engineers are the main guard against low-quality, AI-generated output, and that doesn't scale.** A review-only guard scales linearly with volume — more PRs means more reviewing — so as agent-written code grows it just catches more slop, rather than reducing how much slop is produced. The knowledge of "what good looks like" lives in a few people's heads and a manually maintained rule list, instead of in a durable, shared, improving asset.

We need to evolve this into a **continuous engineering quality loop** built around one shared knowledge source: capture senior judgment as reusable entries; apply that same source both at write-time (to prevent issues) and at review-time (to catch them); mine recurring patterns and real outcomes into validated new guardrails; and retire or refine rules that stop earning their place. The system should improve over time while staying bounded by human review, clear rule ownership, and verification — so it **raises code quality rather than accelerating low-quality output.**

## Goal

Build an agent-assisted engineering quality system that externalizes senior engineering judgment into a single, self-improving knowledge library, and applies it across the lifecycle. From that one source the system should:

* **Prevent** problems at write-time by surfacing the relevant guidance to developers and agents as they build, and making the right pattern the default (the primary scaling lever).
* **Catch** the residue at review-time — code-quality, architecture, security, testing, frontend, backend, and documentation issues — with review depth scaled to the change's risk.
* **Educate** by explaining the _why and the trade-off_ behind each finding, so contributors (human and AI) develop judgment, not just compliance.
* **Learn** from two signals — senior decisions and real outcomes (bugs, reverts, incidents) — proposing new, refined, promoted, or retired guardrails, always through human approval.
* **Automate fixes** where confidence and verification are strong.

Fixes follow a **risk-tiered model**: mechanical auto-fixes first, then higher-value semantic fixes and bounded refactors, where broader changes require stronger evidence, clearer scope, and tighter human approval.

Success is measured by **slop produced going down over time** (and rising agreement with our best engineers' decisions) — not by catch-rate going up. A healthy system makes the guard quieter, because prevention moved upstream.

## Non-Goals

These are out of scope _for now_ — and deliberately so. They are **gated behind trust and verification, not excluded forever**: the same guardrails and metrics this epic builds are what would later make them safe.

* **Fully autonomous feature delivery, bug fixing, incident triage** — while this is not part of the epic, it is a NORTH STAR we are going towards. This epic is an enabler along with automated UI testing.
* **Large-scale automatic refactoring of existing code.**

Additionally, the system never silently changes its own rules: all learned guardrails are _proposals_ that pass through human ownership and approval.

# Task Breakdown (draft)

1. **Build the knowledge library + authoring/approval gate**

**Deliver:** the structured store of judgment entries (schema, storage, versioning), the flow by which an entry comes to exist and gets an owner, and a small hand-seeded starter set — enough to build and test #2/#3/#4 before the learning loop exists.

**Grounded example:** an entry for "use Effect's error channel, don't throw" carries the principle, the why, a Good and a Bad snippet, its scope (`backend`), severity, and whether it's auto-fixable. A senior writes it once; it then drives _both_ the coding-agent hint (#3) and the reviewer's check (#4).

**Already in the repo:** `.opencode/skills/pr-rules/` is a working v0 — \~50 entries as `.md` files with frontmatter (`id`, `severity`, `scope`, `auto-fixable`) and What/Why/Good/Bad/Fix-Hint bodies; [\_categories.md](https://claude.ai/epitaxy/.opencode/skills/pr-rules/_categories.md) is the schema spec, [\_index.md](https://claude.ai/epitaxy/.opencode/skills/pr-rules/_index.md) the manifest. **Gap:** schema lacks confidence/provenance/owner fields; the index is hand-maintained and drifts; no approval step distinct from a normal PR.

**Boundary:** owns the store + the author/own/approve gate — **not** automated discovery from history (that's #6, whose proposals pass through this gate). Content only — not retrieval (#2) or application (#3/#4).

**R&D:** the entry schema (fields serving both injection and review); the authoring/approval workflow and conflict resolution; which tacit entries to seed first.

**Net:** the container + the gate every entry passes through. Lock the schema first.

Separate knowledge base into architectural (high-level) and coding (concrete rules, frameworks, etc.)

Maybe go over old PRs and check commit history and PR review comments to see what can we extract for initial ruleset

We need to solve what we apply for execution and what for review as in: for example skills for a running agent vs rule for review agent

Nested AGENTS.md? How do we solve drift?

Initially gate - human? We collect data on human decision and eventually automate the gate based on past data.

---

2. **Build the retrieval service ("what's relevant here")**

**Deliver:** a service that takes a file or diff and returns the relevant slice of the #1 library plus relevant code context, by indexing what already exists — the live repo (structure, imports, types), the #1 library, and the ADRs produced by #5. Authors no context docs of its own.

**Grounded example:** exactly your framing — for a PR touching only `packages/frontend-app/**`, decide the frontend + universal entries apply but the backend Effect entries don't; finer-grained, flag that an auth-touching file makes the `frontend-app-persistence-security` entry relevant. It hands those entries to the reviewer; it doesn't decide if they're violated.

**Already in the repo:** the scope-folder loader in [\_categories.md](https://claude.ai/epitaxy/.opencode/skills/pr-rules/_categories.md) — `universal/` always, `frontend/` when frontend files change, `backend/` for backend, `architecture/` when a PR touches >5 files or adds files. That _is_ retrieval, just coarse (by folder/path, whole-PR). **Gap:** per-change relevance and ranking, and pulling _code_ context, not just rule files.

**Boundary:** indexes existing/derived sources — does **not** hand-maintain a codemap (the folder structure is the codemap). Surfaces candidates — does **not** judge violations. Consumes ADRs from #5; never generates them.

**R&D:** retrieval method (path/scope vs. import-graph vs. embeddings vs. hybrid); how much context is derivable from code vs. needs a doc; output budget.

**Net:** pure plumbing — an index plus a relevance query — that keeps write-time and review pulling the _same_ knowledge.

‌

---

3. **Apply the library at write-time (prevention)**

**Deliver:** the library wired into feature creation for developers and AI agents — scoped context injection (via #2), scaffolds/templates for common work, and deterministic hooks for mechanical rules. For a pre-push check it **invokes #4's engine locally** rather than building its own.

**Grounded example:** an agent editing a Tamagui screen gets the design-token rule + the simplicity gate injected _before_ it writes; if it hardcodes a hex, a pre-commit hook blocks the commit; a "new admin feature module" scaffold ships with i18n and a Storybook story already wired, so the conventions are the default, not an afterthought.

**Already in the repo:** the [AGENTS.md](https://claude.ai/epitaxy/AGENTS.md) kernels (root + package) are injected as agent guidance — [CLAUDE.md](https://claude.ai/epitaxy/CLAUDE.md), `.junie/guidelines.md`, and `opencode.jsonc` all redirect to them; `.pre-commit-config.yaml` + `lint-staged` enforce mechanical rules (secret detection, formatting, terraform) at commit time. **Gap:** the injected guidance is the whole static kernel, not per-change entries from #2; no scaffolds; no pre-push invocation of the review engine.

**Boundary:** prevention only (inject, scaffold, mechanical hooks). Does **not** build review logic — that lives in #4 and is called here. Consumes #1 via #2.

**R&D:** which surface per entry (hint vs. hook vs. scaffold, driven by confidence); staying non-intrusive; what the pre-push pass surfaces vs. defers to PR review.

**Net:** the main scaling lever — stops slop at creation; reuses #4's engine instead of a second reviewer.

First trigger: asynchronous background loop continuously analyzing a running coding session  
Second trigger: on session end or on compaction or on timestamp (every 5 minutes)  
Third trigger: deterministic hook on a certain stye violation

---

4. **Improve the GitHub review + fix agents**

**Deliver:** a reusable **review/fix engine** plus its GitHub integration — risk-based triage that scales depth to the change, focused specialists composed per scope, one synthesized de-duplicated review, and tiered auto-fix (mechanical → verified-semantic → bounded-refactor) — all reading #1 via #2. Callable by #3 for its local pass; its triage signal is reused by #5.

**Grounded example:** a PR is marked ready → the agent loads the scoped rules, posts a structured verdict with findings and a `/oc fix` offer; commenting `/oc fix` triggers the fix agent, which applies the auto-fixable findings as atomic commits and runs `pnpm format` + `type-check`.

**Already in the repo:** the most built-out area — [pr-review.md](https://claude.ai/epitaxy/.opencode/agent/pr-review.md), [pr-fix.md](https://claude.ai/epitaxy/.opencode/agent/pr-fix.md), [docs-review.md](https://claude.ai/epitaxy/.opencode/agent/docs-review.md), wired via `.github/workflows/pr-review.yml` / `pr-fix.yml` / `docs-review.yml`. It already has depth modes (Focused/Standard/Hybrid by diff size), auto re-review on push, loop prevention, and auto-fixable gating. **Gap vs. the vision:** one monolithic reviewer (not parallel specialists); read-only, so it can't run tests to self-verify a finding; triage is diff-_size_, not risk-aware (auth/money/migration); fix tier is mechanical-only.

**Boundary:** reads the _same_ library as #3 (no separate rule set). Reviews and fixes; doesn't author knowledge — new patterns go to #6.

**R&D:** triage signals (paths, size, auth/money/migration/new deps; deterministic vs. LLM); specialist composition + a synthesizer noise budget; what evidence justifies each auto-fix tier.

**Net:** the authoritative guard — technical hardening of what you already run, reused by #3.

---

5. **Capture durable artifacts from merged changes (changelog + ADR generation)**

**Deliver:** at PR-ready / merge time, generate (a) a changelog/release-note entry for every change, and (b) a **draft ADR** for changes the triage flags as architecturally significant — both human-reviewable before they land. ADRs are written to a location #2 indexes.

**Grounded example:** a PR that swaps the job queue gets a one-line changelog entry automatically; because it touches an architectural boundary, it also gets a draft ADR — "chose X over SQS, because throughput/ordering, trade-off Z" — pre-filled from the diff + PR body for an owner to confirm. Next month, a reviewer working nearby has that rationale surfaced by #2 instead of re-litigating it.

**Already in the repo:** changelog has a foundation — `.changeset/` is wired and [docs/product/09-release-notes.md](https://claude.ai/epitaxy/docs/product/09-release-notes.md) is the product-facing target (docs-review already has rules keeping release notes lean). **ADRs are greenfield** — there's no `docs/adr/` yet; the architecture skills already _expect_ one, so this creates the source they reference.

**Boundary:** captures _per-change instances_ (descriptive) — **not** generalizable rules (that's #6); it's a _signal source_ for #6. Generates drafts; humans approve rationale (a wrong recorded "why" is worse than none). Reuses #4's triage for ADR-worthiness — no separate significance classifier.

**R&D:** the trigger (lean on #4's risk signal vs. its own heuristic); draft quality (inferable from diff + PR body vs. must ask the author); where ADRs live + format so #2 indexes and #6 mines them. For ADRs to be discoverable we need to enforce good “why“ comments (not “what“ comments) in #3 and #4

**Net:** turns each merged change into durable, retrievable context — feeding #2's architectural awareness and #6's learning, while keeping changelog noise low and ADR rationale honest.

---

6. **Build the learning loop (mining + initial backfill)**

**Deliver:** a pipeline that mines recurring review findings and real outcomes (bugs, reverts, incidents, dismissed findings, and the ADRs/changelogs from #5) into **proposed** entries, edits, promotions, or retirements — each routed through #1's approval gate. Its first run is a **backfill over existing history** to bulk-populate the library.

**Grounded example:** a backfill run reads the last several months of human PR comments + reverts, notices reviewers keep flagging "authz logic in the controller" and "console.log left in," and opens a PR proposing two entries (one new, one already covered by `no-console-log`) for an owner to approve.

**Already in the repo:** nothing automated for code rules — **greenfield.** But the _pattern_ is proven in-house on the product side: [docs/question-quality-control.md](https://claude.ai/epitaxy/docs/question-quality-control.md) runs an LLM-as-judge that regenerates failed quiz questions _with feedback examples_ and a _backfill_ safety net. Same shape (judge → feedback → backfill) — worth borrowing.

**Boundary:** owns automated discovery; #1 owns the store and approval. Proposes only — owners approve; never silently mutates. Blends two signals (judgment + outcomes); doesn't review or fix.

**R&D:** signal sources + clustering (real pattern vs. noise); validating a proposal before it ships (e.g. replay against past PRs); promotion/pruning criteria + backfill reach.

**Net:** the automated populator — ongoing engine _and_ initial fill. Ongoing learning needs #4's findings, but the backfill run can start earlier since it only needs history.

---

7. **Define + instrument success metrics**

**Deliver:** a metrics pipeline tracking agreement with senior decisions, slop-at-generation trend, and false-positive/dismiss rates — on a dashboard, defining the thresholds that gate how much autonomy #3, #4, and #6 get.

**Grounded example:** per-rule, the dashboard shows acceptance vs. dismissal — `no-hardcoded-hex` at 98% accepted (safe to keep auto-fixing), a noisier rule at 40% (flag for pruning) — and a trend line of mechanical findings-per-PR falling as #3's prevention ramps.

**Already in the repo:** only the `Review Meta` footer in [pr-review.md](https://claude.ai/epitaxy/.opencode/agent/pr-review.md) (rules-loaded count, scopes, model) — telemetry, not metrics. No acceptance tracking, trend, or agreement measurement — **greenfield.** Nearest in-house analog is again the pass/fail judge in [question-quality-control.md](https://claude.ai/epitaxy/docs/question-quality-control.md).

**Boundary:** **defines** metrics + gating thresholds; #4 and #6 **enforce** the gates that read them. Measures the system; doesn't make review/fix decisions.

**R&D:** labelling ground truth ("good vs. slop", "agrees with senior") cheaply; which metric gates which step; attributing prevention (#3) vs. detection (#4) so you can see slop dropping upstream.

**Net:** the control system — without it, "self-improving" and "less slop" are unverifiable, so stand it up early.

Measure of certain PR comments disappear with time (like return types in Typescript)

---

**Cross-cutting notes (not tasks):**

* **Design rule:** #3 and #4 both consume the #1 library through #2, and #3 reuses #4's engine — that's the guarantee write-time and review enforce the same taste.
* **Build order:** #1 + #2 (lock the schema) → #3 and #4 in parallel → #5 (artifacts) → #6 (learning — mines #5's ADRs/changelogs plus #4's findings; its backfill can start earlier on history) → with #7 (metrics) stood up early throughout.
* **Maturity read:** #4 is \~60% there; #1/#2/#3 exist in crude form; #5 is partial (changesets wired, ADRs greenfield); #6/#7 are greenfield. Highest-leverage early work: harden the schema (#1) and replace folder-scoping with real retrieval (#2) — everything compounds off those two.

fields.description:
Once a course has been created and finalized through the chat-based generation flow, creators currently have no way to go back and edit an individual Level's content. This ticket adds the ability to open, modify, and re-save a Level post-finalization — optionally showing a diff to highlight what changed compared to the originally generated content.

---

**Given** a course has been finalized,

**When** a creator opens a Level from the course overview,

**Then** the Level content is shown in an editable state and the creator can make changes.

---

**Given** a creator has made changes to a Level,

**When** they save the edits,

**Then** the updated content is reflected in the course without requiring the entire course to be re-generated.

---

**Given** a Level has been edited and saved,

**When** the creator views the Level (optional / stretch: with a diff view enabled),

**Then** they can clearly see what was changed versus the originally generated content.

---

fields.description:
When a user uploads a PDF as a source, the generated course currently ignores any images it contains. This ticket adds a pipeline to extract images from uploaded PDFs, store them, generate a contextual description per image, and have the agent write image placeholders (e.g. \[image 2\]) at relevant points in the artifact. Once generation is complete, each placeholder is deterministically replaced with the actual stored image in the final course output.

**Pipeline:** PDF Upload → Image Extraction → Storage Bucket → Caption/Contextual Description per image → Agent writes image placeholders where relevant → Placeholders replaced with actual images in final course.

---

**Given** a PDF containing images is uploaded as a source,

**When** the course generation pipeline processes the PDF,

**Then** images are extracted, stored in a bucket, and each image has a contextual description generated that the agent can reference.

---

**Given** images have been extracted and described from the source PDF,

**When** the agent generates Level content,

**Then** the agent writes image placeholders (e.g. \[image 2\]) in the content at points where the corresponding image is contextually relevant.

---

**Given** a generated artifact contains image placeholders,

**When** the course is finalized,

**Then** each placeholder is replaced with its corresponding image from storage, so the final course displays the actual images inline.

---

**Given** one or more sources are used during course generation,

**When** the course is finalized,

**Then** each source is assigned a numbered reference (e.g. \[1\], \[2\]) and a source list is included in the course.

**Then** relevant passages include inline citation references (e.g. \[1\]) that link back to the corresponding source.

---

**Given** a PDF is used as a source,

**When** citations are generated,

**Then** the PDF is assigned its own source number and citations pointing to it appear specifically in the course content where that PDF's material was used.

fields.summary: Create test markdown file at repo root

issuetype.description: Tasks track small, distinct pieces of work.
issuetype.name: Task

fields.description:
A new markdown file must be created at the root of the monorepo. This is a test file to validate the file-creation pipeline end-to-end.

\*\*Requirements (from Slack thread C0BD13V0WG6 / 1782457756.850679):\*\*  
\- File location: repo root (\`/\`)  
\- File format: Markdown (\`.md\`)  
\- File content: must contain exactly the text \`this is a test file\`

\## Acceptance Criteria  
\- \[ \] A \`.md\` file exists at the repository root (e.g. \`test.md\`)  
\- \[ \] The file contains the text \`this is a test file\`  
\- \[ \] No other files are added, modified, or deleted  
\- \[ \] \`pnpm type-check\` exits 0  
\- \[ \] \`pnpm test\` exits 0

\## Implementation Spec (plan-agent)  
\# Implementation Spec: Root-Level Test Markdown File

\## Overview

Add a single static Markdown file to the repository root. No logic, no dependencies, no build changes — this is a pure file-creation task whose primary purpose is validating the file-creation pipeline itself.

\---

\## Approach

Create one new file. Touch nothing else. The constraints on \`pnpm type-check\` and \`pnpm test\` passing are satisfied by default, since a \`.md\` file carries no TypeScript or runtime surface.

\---

\## Major Steps

1\. \*\*Create the file\*\* at the repository root with the name \`test.md\`.  
2\. \*\*Write exactly the required content\*\* (see Content Contract below).  
3\. \*\*Verify no other files are staged\*\* before committing.

\---

\## Content Contract

The file must contain the following text. Trailing newline is acceptable and conventional; no other content should be present.

\`\`\`  
this is a test file  
\`\`\`

\> \*\*Exact-match note:\*\* The acceptance criteria says "contains the text", not "equals the text", so a single trailing newline (\`\\n\`) is safe. Do \*\*not\*\* add headings, frontmatter, extra whitespace, or any other characters.

\---

\## Data / Contract Changes

| Dimension | Change |  
|---|---|  
| New files | \`test.md\` (repo root) |  
| Modified files | None |  
| Deleted files | None |  
| TypeScript types | None |  
| API / schema | None |  
| Build config | None |  
| Dependencies | None |

\---

\## Edge Cases & Constraints

| Scenario | Mitigation |  
|---|---|  
| A \`test.md\` already exists at the root | Check before creating; if present, verify content matches exactly rather than overwriting blindly |  
| Monorepo tooling (e.g., Turborepo, Nx) treats \`\*.md\` files as inputs to some task | Confirm task hashing is unaffected; a root-level \`.md\` should not invalidate any package's cache |  
| Linters configured to lint Markdown (e.g., \`markdownlint\`) | Run any configured Markdown linter locally; the one-line content is trivially lint-clean, but confirm no rule requires a trailing heading or blank line |  
| \`.gitignore\` or \`.npmignore\` patterns that might exclude \`\*.md\` at root | Verify the file will actually be tracked by Git — \`git status\` should show it as a new untracked file before staging |  
| Line-ending policy (\`autocrlf\`, \`.editorconfig\`) | Ensure the file is committed with \`LF\` endings to avoid spurious diffs on Windows contributors |

\---

\## Testing Strategy

Because this change contains no executable code, the testing strategy is verification-oriented rather than unit-test-oriented.

\### 1. Automated CI Gates (already required by AC)

\`\`\`  
pnpm type-check   # must exit 0  
pnpm test         # must exit 0  
\`\`\`

Both should pass unchanged, since a \`.md\` file introduces no TypeScript or test subjects. If either fails after this change, the root cause is environmental, not this file.

\### 2. File-Existence Check

Add (or rely on an existing) pipeline step that asserts:

\`\`\`  
\# Pseudocode — adapt to whatever shell/script runner CI uses  
assert file_exists("test.md")  
assert file_contains("test.md", "this is a test file")  
\`\`\`

If the pipeline has a dedicated "file-creation validation" stage (the stated purpose of this ticket), this is where it runs.

\### 3. Diff Hygiene Check

In CI or during PR review, confirm the diff contains \*\*exactly one file addition\*\* with \*\*exactly one content line\*\* (plus optional trailing newline). Any broader diff is a red flag.

\### 4. Manual Spot-Check (pre-merge)

\- \`git diff --stat\` shows only \`test.md | 1 +\`  
\- \`cat test.md\` prints \`this is a test file\`  
\- \`git status\` shows no other modified, deleted, or untracked files

\---

\## Non-Goals

\- This file is not documentation and should not be linked from \`README.md\` or any index.  
\- No logic should read or import this file at runtime.  
\- This spec does not cover cleanup/deletion of the file post-validation — that is a separate ticket decision.

fields.summary: Evaluate safe, isolated AI coding agent workflows

issuetype.description: Tasks track small, distinct pieces of work.
issuetype.name: Task

fields.description:
# Problem

We want developers and AI coding agents to work on Uniplay tasks productively without giving agents unsafe access to the main local worktree, host filesystem, secrets, Docker socket, cloud credentials, or protected branches.

[PR #771](https://github.com/UniplayIO/uniplay/pull/771) explored one version of this idea: a first-party `uniplay agent` CLI that starts an OpenCode Docker container with the repo mounted. The original vision was useful: make agent usage reproducible, easy to start, and integrated with Uniplay workflows. However, a custom long-lived Compose wrapper may not be the best path if our primary goal is isolation, safety, and low maintenance.

We should reframe the work around the underlying problem: **safe agent execution with minimal custom infrastructure**, using existing standards and products wherever possible.

# Goal

Design a developer-friendly AI agent workflow that:

* Runs agents in isolated, disposable environments.
* Prevents accidental destructive changes to the real local worktree.
* Avoids mounting secrets or host credentials by default.
* Produces reviewable patches, branches, or PRs before changes land.
* Uses established tools such as devcontainers, Codespaces, Copilot coding agent, Docker sandboxing, or similar existing solutions before building custom Uniplay tooling.
* Keeps any Uniplay-specific wrapper thin and focused on policy, not reimplementing agent lifecycle management.

# Non-Goals

* Do not build a full custom agent platform unless existing options fail clear requirements.
* Do not make a long-lived privileged local container the default agent environment.
* Do not mount `~/.ssh`, `.env`, cloud credentials, Docker socket, or the main worktree into an agent by default.
* Do not require one specific AI provider or editor unless justified by usability and safety.

# Options To Evaluate

* GitHub Copilot coding agent for issue-to-PR workflows.
* GitHub Codespaces with devcontainer-based isolation.
* Local VS Code/Cursor devcontainer workflows.
* DevPod or Coder for portable devcontainer environments.
* Docker Sandboxes / hardened Docker isolation.
* E2B, Modal, or similar sandbox APIs for future hosted agent execution.
* A thin `uniplay agent` wrapper that creates disposable worktrees and returns patches, only if existing tooling is insufficient.

# Security / Safety Requirements

* Agent runs in a disposable environment.
* Main repo is not mounted writable by default.
* Secrets are opt-in and scoped.
* Network access is explicit by mode.
* Agent cannot push to protected branches.
* Human approval is required before applying patches or opening/merging PRs.
* Generated changes are inspectable as a diff.
* Resource limits are defined where possible.
* Any local API must bind to localhost only.

# User Experience Requirements

* A developer can start the workflow with one or two documented commands.
* The workflow works for common Uniplay tasks: code edits, tests, docs, PR fixes.
* Failure modes are understandable: missing Docker, missing auth, failed tests, blocked network.
* The default recommendation is clear: “Use X for normal work; use Y for advanced/local isolation.”

# Acceptance Criteria

* Document the recommended agent workflow for Uniplay.
* Compare at least three existing solutions against safety, usability, cost, maintenance, and integration effort.
* Recommend one default path and one fallback/local path.
* Define minimum isolation policy for agent execution.
* Define how agents produce reviewable output: patch, branch, or PR.
* Define what credentials, if any, may be exposed to the agent.
* Create a proof-of-concept using an existing solution before proposing custom CLI code.
* Document why any custom Uniplay wrapper is necessary, if recommended.
* Include migration notes from the dropped `uniplay agent` PR vision.

# Original Vision To Preserve

The dropped PR was aiming for:

* A simple first-party command for agent workflows.
* Reproducible agent runtime.
* OpenCode/Codex-style coding assistance inside a controlled environment.
* Persistent agent sessions/auth.
* Easy status/session visibility.
* A workflow developers could discover from `uniplay --help`.

We should preserve that product intent, but solve it through safer and more standard foundations first.

issuetype.description: Tasks track small, distinct pieces of work.
issuetype.name: Task

fields.description:
## Goal

The mobile app must be able to ask the learner for notification permission, obtain a push token from Expo, and register it with the backend so the backend knows where to send future pushes for this user.

## Acceptance criteria

**Given** a learner opens the app for the first time after logging in
**When** the app asks for notification permission and the learner grants it
**Then** the app obtains a push token and the backend stores it as an active device for this user

**Given** a learner has denied notification permission on iOS
**When** the app's push setup runs
**Then** the learner is shown a message explaining how to enable notifications in Settings, not a re-prompt (iOS does not allow re-prompting)

**Given** a learner who previously registered a push token logs out and a different user logs in on the same phone
**When** the new user's app registers its push token
**Then** the token is transferred to the new user and the previous user no longer receives pushes on that device

**Given** a learner has granted notification permission
**When** the backend is asked to look up their active devices
**Then** the registered token is returned and marked as active

## Details

* Android requires a notification channel to be created before the permission prompt, otherwise Android silently drops pushes.
* The permission explainer should be shown once per user (not every app launch).
* Device registration happens after a successful login.

fields.description:
## Goal

Build the core push notification platform so the app can deliver push notifications to users' phones when specific events happen in the product. This is the enabling work for [UPENG-1189](https://uniplayio.atlassian.net/browse/UPENG-1189) (new course published → push to tenant members) and for future notification types.

## Scope

* Mobile app registers each installation's push token with the backend.
* Backend can deliver a push notification to a registered user's phone via Expo + APNs/FCM.
* New course publication triggers a push to the tenant's members.
* Tapping a push opens the relevant screen in the app.

## Out of scope (future work)

* In-app notification inbox
* Per-category user preferences / opt-out toggles
* Any notification kinds beyond "new course published" (future reminders, streaks, level-ups, coin-spend, etc. are tracked on their own stories under the Continuous Learning epic)

## Acceptance criteria

**Given** a learner has the mobile app installed and granted notification permission
**When** an admin publishes a new course in their tenant
**Then** the learner's phone receives a push notification about the new course, and tapping it opens that course in the app

See subtasks for the individual pieces and their per-step acceptance criteria.

## Problem

The coding agent reads the Jira ticket and then spends its entire session exploring the codebase to understand where and how to implement. This exploration fills its working memory with context it later discards, leaving less room for the actual implementation — and the agent may still miss relevant patterns or make choices that don't fit the codebase. Solution design is in excavator-context-engineering.md.

## Acceptance Criteria

**Given** the coding agent receives a ticket to implement

**When** it starts its session

**Then** it begins with a prepared brief describing the relevant codebase areas and patterns

---

**Given** the prepared brief is available

**When** the coding agent works on the implementation

**Then** it does not spend its implementation session on broad codebase exploration

---

**Given** a prepared brief is generated for a ticket

**When** the brief is delivered to the coding agent

**Then** it identifies whether tests exist for the affected area

issuetype.description: Tasks track small, distinct pieces of work.

issuetype.description: Epics track collections of related bugs, stories, and tasks.
issuetype.name: Epic

fields.description:
## Problem

Before the auto-fix agent acts, it waits for the Pi code review to finish. The check fetches all Pi review workflow runs filtered by branch name only — not by the current commit SHA. It then uses an all-or-nothing check: every run on the branch must be in a completed state before the gate clears. This means any run from an earlier commit that is stuck in progress (for example due to a GitHub infrastructure issue) will permanently deadlock the auto-fix loop for the entire branch with no escape path.

## Acceptance Criteria

**Given** the Pi review for the current commit is still running

**When** the auto-fix agent checks whether to proceed

**Then** it waits correctly and does not act prematurely

---

**Given** there are Pi review runs from earlier commits on the same branch

**When** the auto-fix agent checks the Pi review status

**Then** it is not blocked by those older runs

---

**Given** the Pi review for the current commit has completed

**When** the auto-fix agent evaluates the gate

**Then** it proceeds normally

fields.summary: Admin: Drag-to-reorder levels within a course, persisted per company

issuetype.description: Tasks track small, distinct pieces of work.
issuetype.name: Task

fields.description:
Admins editing a course in the admin panel can reorder that course's levels by dragging them up or down within the level list. The new order is saved permanently and is scoped to the company — reordering levels for Company A has no effect on Company B's view of the same course template, if applicable.

Employees using the learner app see and progress through levels in the saved order, without requiring an app update. The admin and employee views of level order are always consistent.

\## Acceptance Criteria  
\- \[ \] When an admin opens a course in the admin panel, the levels list supports drag-and-drop reordering (same interaction pattern used elsewhere in the admin UI).  
\- \[ \] Dragging a level to a new position and saving persists that order — the order is unchanged if the admin refreshes the page or returns to the course on a later date.  
\- \[ \] The saved order is per-company: reordering levels for Company A does not affect Company B's level order for that course.  
\- \[ \] The learner app displays and delivers levels to employees in the admin-saved order without requiring an app update.  
\- \[ \] An employee who opens the course after a reorder sees the new level sequence immediately (server-driven, not cached from a prior app version).  
\- \[ \] If no custom order has been set by an admin, levels display in their original default order for all companies.

\## Feature Spec (plan-agent)  
\# Spec: Company-Scoped Level Reordering for Courses

\## Description

Admins can reorder the levels within a course by dragging them up or down in the admin panel's level list. The resulting order is stored per company, so each company can have its own level sequence for the same underlying course template without affecting any other company. Employees in the learner app see and progress through levels in exactly the order the admin saved — served dynamically so no app update is needed to reflect a change.

\## Acceptance Criteria

\- \[ \] When an admin opens a course in the admin panel, the levels list supports drag-and-drop reordering using the same interaction pattern used elsewhere in the admin UI.  
\- \[ \] Dragging a level to a new position and saving persists that order; the order is unchanged if the admin refreshes the page or returns to the course on a later session.  
\- \[ \] The saved order is scoped to the admin's company: reordering levels for Company A has no effect on Company B's level order for the same course.  
\- \[ \] If no custom order has been saved by an admin for a given company, levels display in the original default order for that company.  
\- \[ \] The learner app displays levels to employees in the admin-saved order, served from the backend so no app update is required to reflect a reorder.  
\- \[ \] An employee who opens a course after a reorder immediately sees the new sequence; no stale ordering from a prior session or app version is shown.  
\- \[ \] The level order seen by an admin in the admin panel and the level order delivered to employees in the learner app are always consistent for the same company.

\## Out of Scope

\- Reordering levels across courses or reordering content within a level.  
\- Any per-employee or per-cohort customization of level order (scope is company only).  
\- Migrating or reconciling in-progress employee completions when an admin reorders levels (not addressed in the discussion).

\## Definition of Done

A reviewer walks through the following:

1\. \*\*Admin panel — basic reorder and persist.\*\* Open a course as an admin, drag one level from its current position to a different position, and save. Refresh the page and confirm the level appears in the new position. Return to the course in a new browser session and confirm the order is still correct.

2\. \*\*Company isolation.\*\* Log in as an admin for Company B and open the same course. Confirm the level order matches Company B's own saved order (or the default if none has been set), not the order set by Company A's admin.

3\. \*\*Default order fallback.\*\* Open a course for a company where no reorder has ever been saved. Confirm levels appear in their original default order.

4\. \*\*Learner app consistency.\*\* As an employee of Company A, open the course in the learner app after an admin reorder has been saved. Confirm the levels appear in the same sequence the admin set — without installing an app update.

5\. \*\*Immediate reflection.\*\* With the learner app already open (or after a fresh open), confirm the updated sequence is visible right away after the admin saves a reorder, with no residual stale ordering.

fields.summary: Add path-scoped rules specifically for Codex in main repo

issuetype.description: Tasks track small, distinct pieces of work.

fields.summary: AI Excavator: Code Action aka AGI

issuetype.description: Epics track collections of related bugs, stories, and tasks.
issuetype.name: Epic

fields.description:
## Description

Codex doesn't support path-scoped rules, unlike Claude Code and Cursor. However, they do have a configuration file where you can define alternative names for markdown files that should be automatically loaded (basically forcing Codex to auto-load `MYNAMEHERE.md` when it works in a folder.

This is important because our system is built around putting package-specific instructions inside `.claude/rules/*.md`, `.cursor/rules/*.md`, `.opencode/rules/*.md`, etc. Since AGENTS.md files are auto-loaded by all harnesses, I had to avoid that filename to avoid loading duplicate instructions.

Therefore, I decided on the names `CODEX_SPECIFIC_OVERRIDE.md`. These are basically the equivalent of `.{harness}/rules/*.md`, but for Codex.

## **Instructions to set up the Codex instruction overrides**

In order to make Codex automatically read these files, you need to add `CODEX_SPECIFIC_OVERRIDE.md` to your `config.toml`. Luckily, the `uniplay-ai` CLI will do this for you.  

* Pull the latest version of the `uniplayIO/ai-tooling` repo
* Re-run `uniplay-ai install`.

This will add necessary configurations to your `.codex/config.toml` so you can forget about it.

Note: Difficulty level is something we need to investigate. How can we support different difficulty levels for the same course? The agent should be able to suggest whether levels cover different parts of the course or whether the difficulty should increase from one level to the next.

Multi-agent system that turns Slack feature requests into reviewed PRs.
Part of the Agentic Engineering Quality System epic (UPENG-1918).

# Pipeline (built, UPENG-2039–2042 done)

1. **pm-agent** — separate Slack bot that only writes to Jira (UPENG-2076).
2. **plan-agent** — plans from the request; exploration agent grounds it
   in the codebase (UPENG-2069); plan-agent measurably improves
   code-agent output (UPENG-2070).
3. **code-agent** — code → PR → auto-fix loop; I/O migrated to the
   Effect platform (UPENG-2046); can fetch screenshots from Slack
   threads (UPENG-2058).
4. **Review** — Pi review gate (UPENG-2068), PR-review agent with
   feedback loop under evaluation (UPENG-1991), OpenAI models usable
   for review (UPENG-2016).

# Status (2026-07-09)

End-to-end pipeline tested on a real feature request (UPENG-2041);
deployment in progress (UPENG-2075). Competes for my time with
[Agent-Driven Course Creation](/projects/agent-driven-course-creation.md).
Hard-won context on why this is difficult:
[multi-agent systems reality check](/notes/multi-agent-systems-reality-check.md).

---
type: Note
title: Multi-agent systems reality check
description: Why "AI company" multi-agent systems underdeliver — coordination, shared context, and model-tier economics.
tags: [agents, llm, opinion]
timestamp: 2026-07-09T13:00:00Z
---

My position as of 2026-07-08, from building
[Excavator](/projects/excavator.md):

1. **Coordination doesn't scale.** Getting one agent to collaborate on
   a single task is already hard; 5+ agents acting as "an entire
   company" with shared context is practically unfeasible — especially
   on a large codebase. Whole startups selling "AI companies" still
   barely have real multi-agent systems, for this reason.
2. **Model-tier economics dominate quality.** Constant cost-efficiency
   pressure makes the idea self-defeating: a working pipeline needs
   top-tier models (Fable/Opus-class) throughout; mid-tier models are
   not good enough for agentic pipeline steps.
3. **Stop reinventing the wheel.** Recurring failure mode in our
   approach: rebuilding orchestration primitives that already exist.

Context that day: merged RAG and landed ~20 refactoring commits
(1000+ lines).

# Citations

[1] [DM thread, 2026-07-08](https://uniplayio.slack.com/archives/D0APP6LB0US)
